Position Sizing & The 2% Rule

Illustration for position sizing & the 2% rule.

Illustration for position sizing & the 2% rule.

Position sizing converts chosen assumptions into an exposure. The often-mentioned 2% rule is a heuristic, not an appropriate loss limit for every person or trade. A planned exit can be missed, and losses can exceed the worksheet assumption.

💡
Example

Choose a hypothetical $100,000 account and a 2% planned loss amount: $100,000 × 0.02 = $2,000. With an assumed $100 entry and $95 exit, the $5 difference gives $2,000 ÷ $5 = 400 shares and $40,000 purchase notional before fees. This quantity is a calculation, not a recommendation.

Specify entry, assumed exit, available cash, units and transaction costs.
Check affordability separately: a worksheet quantity is not automatically an executable order.
Repeat with a worse fill: 400 shares sold at $90 lose $4,000 before costs, twice the planned amount.
Include existing positions when evaluating total exposure; a per-trade number does not cap portfolio losses.
Pro Tip

TradeHQ supports market orders. Keep the hypothetical exit in a journal and compare it with the practice result; writing a stop price does not place a protective stop order.

Stop-Loss & Take-Profit Targets

A real stop order becomes eligible for execution when its trigger condition is met. A stop-market order does not guarantee the trigger price; a stop-limit order can remain unfilled. Exact trigger and handling rules depend on the product and broker.

💡
Example

Suppose a share was bought at $100 with a hypothetical stop trigger of $95. If the next available sale fills at $90, the price loss is $10 per share, not $5. Fees add to the loss. An instruction to exit cannot guarantee a maximum loss.

A take-profit instruction and a trailing stop also depend on execution conditions. Selling some units reduces the remaining exposure after a fill, but a planned target alone does not lock in a gain. A gap can cross both a planned entry and exit level.

Separate trigger price, limit price and actual execution price in a worksheet.
Compare an orderly price path with a gap and an unfilled-limit case.
Record the number of units still held after each assumed partial fill.
Pro Tip

These order types are conceptual in TradeHQ. Use market orders and manual practice exits to study the accounting; the simulator does not implement stop, take-profit or trailing-stop execution.

Understanding Risk-Reward Ratios
Keep the ratio order explicit

If the chosen downside is $100 and upside is $300, risk-to-reward is 1:3 and reward-to-risk is 3:1. Reversing the label reverses the meaning. Planned price distances are not realized outcomes, probabilities or guaranteed fills.

💡
Example

With exactly $300 realized wins and $100 realized losses, three wins and seven losses produce 3 × $300 − 7 × $100 = $200 gross. This selected ten-trade example does not establish a strategy edge. Costs, varying sizes and worse exits change the result.

💡
Example

For those fixed outcomes, gross break-even solves 300p − 100(1 − p) = 0, so p = 25%. At exactly 25%, profit is zero before costs, not positive. A $5 cost per completed trade raises break-even to (100 + 5) ÷ 400 = 26.25% under the same fixed assumptions.

Pro Tip

There is no universal minimum ratio for day or swing trading. A high planned reward distance does not make the target likely. Review realized sizes, costs, sample selection and uncertainty together.

Diversification Strategies
Diversification Strategies

Diversification changes concentration across exposures. It can reduce dependence on one issuer or outcome, but holdings can fall together and correlations change. It cannot guarantee protection from a market decline or permanent loss.

💡
Example

Invented equal-weight portfolio: $50 in A and $50 in B. If A falls 20% and B rises 10%, values become $40 and $55, totaling $95: a 5% portfolio loss. If both fall 20%, total value is $80, a 20% loss. The second case shows why two names are not loss insurance.

Look through fund holdings for overlap with directly held stocks.
Compare weights and shared drivers rather than counting ticker symbols.
Cash, bonds, shares and tokens have different risks; none is assigned a guaranteed stability or return tier here.
Rebalancing restores a chosen weighting rule and can incur fees or taxes; it is not automatically a reason to buy a falling asset.
Pro Tip

Compare hypothetical concentrated and mixed exposures over the same invented shocks. Document why the comparison is limited rather than choosing an allocation from an age label or promised return.
